chapters.title: Unit 11: Congruency and Similarity, Construction of Triangles

lessons.title: Exercise 11.1 (p.154) - Congruent and Similar Triangles
lessons.notes_html:
Two triangles are congruent when they are exactly the same in shape AND size: corresponding angles equal and corresponding sides equal. The congruence tests are SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the included angle) and ASA (two angles and a side). Two triangles are similar when corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in the same ratio — same shape, possibly different size (an enlargement).

Formula: For similar triangles, corresponding sides are proportional: a/a' = b/b' = c/c' = scale factor.

In this exercise: 1. State whether pairs of triangles are congruent or similar, with justification (read from the printed figures).; 2. Prove two triangles congruent given angle B = angle M.

Worked Example: Q.1(iv) — Triangles with sides 3.5 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm and 7 cm, 4 cm, 6 cm: congruent or similar?

Formula used: Compare corresponding sides.

Step 1: 7 = 2 x 3.5; 4 = 2 x 2; 6 = 2 x 3 — every side of the second triangle is exactly double the corresponding side of the first.

Step 2: The sides are in the same ratio (scale factor 2) but NOT equal, so the triangles cannot be congruent.

Answer: Similar — the second triangle is an enlargement of the first with scale factor 2.

Worked Example: Q.2 — Given angle B = angle M, prove triangle ABC is congruent to triangle LMN.

Formula used: SAS criterion.

Step 1: The marked equal sides in the figure give AB = LM and BC = MN.

Step 2: The angle between those sides is given equal: angle B = angle M.

Step 3: Two sides and the INCLUDED angle are equal, so by SAS the triangles are congruent.

Answer: Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle LMN by SAS.

mcqs.q: Two triangles have all corresponding sides 5 cm. They are:
mcqs.why: All three sides of one triangle equal the three sides of the other, so the triangles are exactly the same size and shape — congruent by the SSS criterion.

mcqs.q: Two triangles have the same angles 85, 40 and 55 degrees but no equal side is given. They are:
mcqs.why: Equal corresponding angles guarantee the same SHAPE, but without an equal side the sizes may differ. Same shape, possibly different size = similar, not congruent.

mcqs.q: Triangles with sides 3.5, 2, 3 cm and 7, 4, 6 cm are similar with scale factor:
mcqs.why: 7/3.5 = 2, 4/2 = 2 and 6/3 = 2. Every corresponding side is doubled, so the scale factor is 2 (an enlargement).

mcqs.q: The SAS congruence criterion requires:
options: Two sides and any angle equal
Two sides and the INCLUDED angle equal
Two angles and a side equal
mcqs.why: SAS = Side-Angle-Side: two pairs of equal sides with the angle BETWEEN them (the included angle) equal. An angle that is not between the two sides does not prove congruence in general.

mcqs.q: In Q.2, triangle ABC is congruent to triangle LMN because:
options: AB = LM, BC = MN and the included angle B = angle M (SAS)
All their angles are right angles
mcqs.why: The figure marks AB = LM and BC = MN, and angle B = angle M is given. Angle B is the angle between sides AB and BC, and angle M is between LM and MN — two sides and the included angle, so SAS applies.

mcqs.q: Two triangles each have angles 40 and 70 degrees and corresponding sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm equal. They are:
mcqs.why: Corresponding angles are equal AND corresponding sides are equal, so the triangles are exactly the same in shape and size — congruent (ASA/SSS).

mcqs.q: Congruent figures are always:
mcqs.why: Congruent figures have the same shape and the same size — they are similar figures whose scale factor is exactly 1. So every pair of congruent figures is also similar.

mcqs.q: Which condition does NOT prove two triangles congruent?
options: SAS: two sides and included angle equal
ASA: two angles and a corresponding side equal
mcqs.why: Three equal angles (AAA) prove the same shape only — the triangles could be different sizes (similar). Congruence needs at least one pair of corresponding sides equal, as in SSS, SAS or ASA.

mcqs.q: A triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 cm is enlarged by scale factor 3. The new sides are:
mcqs.why: Multiply each side by the scale factor 3: 3 x 3 = 9, 4 x 3 = 12, 5 x 3 = 15. Enlargement multiplies every length by the same factor.

mcqs.q: For similar triangles, corresponding sides are:
mcqs.why: Similarity means equal corresponding angles and corresponding sides in the same ratio — each side of one triangle is the corresponding side of the other multiplied by one fixed scale factor.

lessons.title: Exercise: Construction of Quadrilaterals (p.160)
lessons.notes_html:
Constructions use only a ruler and compasses. The methods: a parallelogram from two sides and the included angle (the fourth vertex is found with arcs of the two side lengths, since opposite sides are equal); a square from one side (perpendiculars at both ends, arcs of the side length); a rhombus from a side and a diagonal (build the triangle formed by two sides and the diagonal, then complete with arcs); a rectangle from two sides, or a side and the diagonal; a trapezium using a line through a vertex parallel to a base; a kite from two different side lengths and the diagonal between their endpoints (arcs on both sides of the diagonal).

Formula: In a rectangle, (diagonal)^2 = (length)^2 + (width)^2 — Pythagoras gives an unknown side, e.g. diagonal 10 cm and side 8 cm give the other side sqrt(100 - 64) = 6 cm.

In this exercise: 1. Parallelograms.; 2. Squares EAST and WEST.; 3. Rhombuses from side and diagonal.; 4. Rectangles.; 5-6. Trapezia.; 7-8. Kites.

Worked Example: Q.1(i) — Construct parallelogram ABCD with AB = 6 cm, AD = 4 cm, angle A = 45 degrees (construction described).

Step 1: Draw the line segment AB = 6 cm.

Step 2: At A, construct an angle of 45 degrees.

Step 3: With A as centre, draw an arc of radius 4 cm cutting the angle arm at D.

Step 4: With B and D as centres, draw arcs of radii 4 cm and 6 cm respectively, cutting each other at C (opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal).

Step 5: Join B to C and C to D.

Answer: Parallelogram ABCD is constructed — opposite sides parallel and equal.

Worked Example: Q.7 — Construct kite ABCD with AB = 5 cm, BC = 6.5 cm and diagonal AC = 8 cm (construction described).

Step 1: Draw the diagonal AC = 8 cm.

Step 2: With A and C as centres, draw arcs of radii 5 cm and 6.5 cm on one side of AC, cutting each other at B.

Step 3: Repeat the same arcs on the other side of AC, cutting at D.

Step 4: Join A to B, B to C, C to D and D to A.

Answer: Kite ABCD is constructed, with AB = AD = 5 cm and CB = CD = 6.5 cm.

mcqs.q: To construct parallelogram ABCD with AB = 6 cm, AD = 4 cm and angle A = 45 degrees, the fourth vertex C is found by arcs of radii:
options: 6 cm from B and 6 cm from D
4 cm from B and 6 cm from D
4 cm from B and 4 cm from D
mcqs.why: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal: BC = AD = 4 cm and DC = AB = 6 cm. So arcs of radius 4 cm (centre B) and 6 cm (centre D) meet at C.

mcqs.q: To construct square EAST with EA = 6.5 cm, after drawing EA you must construct at E and A:
mcqs.why: Every angle of a square is 90 degrees, so perpendiculars are raised at E and A, and arcs of radius 6.5 cm cut them at S and T; joining S to T completes the square.

mcqs.q: Rhombus MNOP has side MN = 4.2 cm and diagonal MO = 8 cm. In the construction, vertex O is found from M and N with arcs of radii:
options: 8 cm from M and 4.2 cm from N
4.2 cm from M and 8 cm from N
mcqs.why: MO is the diagonal, so the arc from M has radius 8 cm; NO is a side of the rhombus, so the arc from N has radius 4.2 cm. Their intersection is O. (Check the data is possible: 8 < 4.2 + 4.2 = 8.4, so the triangle can be formed.)

mcqs.q: Rectangle LAND has side LA = 8 cm and diagonal AD = 10 cm. The other side LD is:
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras in the right-angled triangle: LD = sqrt(AD^2 - LA^2) = sqrt(100 - 64) = sqrt(36) = 6 cm.

mcqs.q: To construct trapezium ABCD with AB parallel to CD, after building triangle ABC the key step is:
options: Through C, draw a line parallel to AB, and mark D on it with an arc of radius CD
Draw the perpendicular bisector of AB
mcqs.why: A trapezium needs one pair of parallel sides. D must lie on the line through C parallel to AB; an arc of radius CD = 4 cm from C fixes D on that line, then A is joined to D.

mcqs.q: Kite ABCD is constructed from diagonal AC = 8 cm with arcs on BOTH sides of AC. This gives a kite because:
options: AB = AD and CB = CD — two pairs of adjacent equal sides
mcqs.why: Using the same pair of radii (5 cm from A, 6.5 cm from C) on both sides of the diagonal gives B and D mirror images, so AB = AD = 5 cm and CB = CD = 6.5 cm — the defining property of a kite.

mcqs.q: In constructing a square, the arcs that cut the perpendiculars have radius equal to:
mcqs.why: All sides of a square are equal, so with EA as the side, arcs of radius EA (6.5 cm) from E and A cut the perpendiculars at S and T, making ES and AT also 6.5 cm.

mcqs.q: A rhombus has all four sides equal. Rhombus MNOP with MN = 2.8 cm therefore has perimeter:
mcqs.why: Perimeter = 4 x side = 4 x 2.8 = 11.2 cm, since every side of a rhombus equals MN = 2.8 cm.

mcqs.q: For trapezium PQRS (PQ parallel to RS, angle SPQ = 70 degrees, SP = 5.6 cm), S is located by:
options: An arc of 9 cm from Q
Constructing 70 degrees at P and an arc of radius 5.6 cm from P cutting the arm
An arc of 4 cm from P
mcqs.why: Angle SPQ is the angle at P between SP and PQ, and SP = 5.6 cm is the side from P. So construct 70 degrees at P, then an arc of radius 5.6 cm centred at P cuts the arm at S. (The 9 cm arc comes later, from S, to fix R.)

mcqs.q: Rectangle HAND has HA = 7 cm and AN = 4 cm. Its perimeter and area are:
mcqs.why: Perimeter = 2 x (7 + 4) = 22 cm. Area = 7 x 4 = 28 cm^2. Opposite sides of the rectangle are 7 cm and 4 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise: Construction of Triangles (p.163-164)
lessons.notes_html:
Triangles are constructed by SSS (three sides: draw one side, then arcs of the other two lengths from its ends), SAS (two sides and the included angle), ASA (a side and the two angles at its ends — the arms meet at the third vertex), SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) and HS for right-angled triangles (hypotenuse and one side: raise 90 degrees at one end of the given side and cut the arm with an arc of the hypotenuse length). The angle bisectors of a triangle all meet at one point, the in-centre; the perpendicular bisectors of the sides all meet at the circum-centre.

Formula: In the HS constructions, the third side comes from Pythagoras: sqrt(hypotenuse^2 - side^2).

In this exercise: 1. SAS triangle with angle bisectors.; 2. SSS triangle with perpendicular bisectors.; 3-4. SSS triangles.; 5-6. SAS/SSA triangles.; 7-8. ASA triangles.; 9-10. Right-angled triangles by HS.

Worked Example: Q.2 — Construct triangle ABC with AB = 6 cm, BC = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm, with its perpendicular bisectors (described).

Step 1: Draw the line segment AC = 5 cm.

Step 2: With A and C as centres, draw arcs of radii 6 cm and 4 cm respectively, cutting each other at B. Join A to B and B to C (SSS).

Step 3: For each side, draw arcs of radius more than half the side from both ends, above and below, and join the meeting points — that line is the perpendicular bisector.

Step 4: The three perpendicular bisectors meet at one point, the circum-centre.

Answer: Triangle ABC is constructed by SSS, with its perpendicular bisectors drawn. (The book prints 'perpendicular bisector of triangle XYZ' in this answer — a misprint for ABC.)

Worked Example: Q.9 — Construct a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 9 cm and one side 6 cm (described).

Step 1: Draw the given side YZ = 6 cm.

Step 2: At Z, construct an angle of 90 degrees.

Step 3: With Y as centre, draw an arc of radius 9 cm (the hypotenuse) cutting the perpendicular arm at X.

Step 4: Join Y to X.

Answer: Right-angled triangle XYZ is constructed by HS; the third side is sqrt(81 - 36) = sqrt(45) = 6.71 cm.

mcqs.q: The three angle bisectors of a triangle meet at one point called the:
mcqs.why: The angle bisectors meet at the in-centre — the centre of the circle that touches all three sides from inside. The PERPENDICULAR bisectors meet at the circum-centre.

mcqs.q: The three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle's sides meet at the:
mcqs.why: The perpendicular bisectors of the sides are concurrent at the circum-centre, which is equidistant from all three vertices (the centre of the circumscribed circle).

mcqs.q: To construct triangle PQR with PQ = 4 cm, QR = 5 cm, RP = 7 cm (SSS), after drawing RP = 7 cm the arcs are:
options: 5 cm from R and 4 cm from P
4 cm from R and 5 cm from P
mcqs.why: Q is joined to R by QR = 5 cm, so the arc centred at R has radius 5 cm; Q is joined to P by PQ = 4 cm, so the arc centred at P has radius 4 cm. The arcs meet at Q.

mcqs.q: Triangle XYZ is constructed from base XY = 8 cm with angle X = 60 degrees and angle Y = 90 degrees. This is construction by:
mcqs.why: A side (XY) and the two angles at its two ends are given — Angle-Side-Angle. The two constructed angle arms meet at Z.

mcqs.q: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 9 cm and one side 6 cm. The third side is:
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras: third side = sqrt(9^2 - 6^2) = sqrt(81 - 36) = sqrt(45) = 6.71 cm. The hypotenuse is the longest side, so we subtract, not add.

mcqs.q: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 11 cm and one side 7 cm. The third side is:
mcqs.why: Third side = sqrt(11^2 - 7^2) = sqrt(121 - 49) = sqrt(72) = 8.49 cm, by Pythagoras (HS construction).

mcqs.q: To draw the perpendicular bisector of a side, the compass arcs from each end must have radius:
mcqs.why: Arcs of radius MORE than half the side, drawn from both ends above and below, cross each other; joining the two crossing points gives the perpendicular bisector. With half or less, the arcs would not meet properly.

mcqs.q: Triangle XYZ with XY = 5 cm, YZ = 4 cm and the INCLUDED angle XYZ = 60 degrees is constructed by:
mcqs.why: Angle XYZ is the angle at Y between sides XY and YZ — the two given sides include the given angle between them, so this is SAS. (With angle Y = 120 degrees in Q.5 the same method is used.)

mcqs.q: Triangle MNO is given by NO = 8 cm, MN = 9 cm and angle M = 45 degrees. Angle M is NOT between the two given sides, so this is construction by:
options: SSA (two sides and a non-included angle)
mcqs.why: Angle M belongs to sides MN and MO; the given sides are MN and NO, so the angle is not included between them. The construction draws MN, makes 45 degrees at M, and cuts the arm with an arc of radius NO = 8 cm from N — SSA.

mcqs.q: Before constructing triangle ABC with sides AB = 4 cm, BC = 6 cm, CA = 9 cm, the triangle inequality check is:
options: 4 + 6 = 10 > 9, so the triangle can be formed
mcqs.why: The sum of any two sides must exceed the third: 4 + 6 = 10 > 9, 4 + 9 > 6 and 6 + 9 > 4. All hold, so the SSS construction works — the arcs meet.

lessons.title: Exercise: Rotation (p.166-167)
lessons.notes_html:
A rotation turns a shape about a fixed point, the centre of rotation, through a given angle in a given direction. About the origin, the coordinate rules are: 90 degrees clockwise: (x, y) goes to (y, -x); 180 degrees (either direction): (x, y) goes to (-x, -y); 270 degrees clockwise (= 90 degrees anticlockwise): (x, y) goes to (-y, x). To FIND a centre of rotation, join each vertex to its image and draw the perpendicular bisectors of the joining segments — they all meet at the centre.

Formula: 90 degrees clockwise: (x, y) -> (y, -x). 180 degrees: (x, y) -> (-x, -y). 270 degrees clockwise: (x, y) -> (-y, x).

In this exercise: 1-2. Rotate triangles by 90 degrees clockwise and 180 degrees.; 3. Rotate single points 90 degrees clockwise.; 4-5. Rotate a square and a triangle (example vertices given).; 6-7. Rotate point P by 90, 180 and 270 degrees.; 8. Find the centre of rotation. (Parts Q.1(a) and Q.2(b) show grid figures without labelled coordinates, so they are done by the same rules.)

Worked Example: Q.1(b) — Rotate triangle A(-2, 1), B(3, 2), C(1, 5) through 90 degrees clockwise about the origin.

Formula used: (x, y) -> (y, -x).

Step 1: A(-2, 1) -> (1, 2).

Step 2: B(3, 2) -> (2, -3).

Step 3: C(1, 5) -> (5, -1). Plot A', B', C' and join them.

Answer: The image has vertices A'(1, 2), B'(2, -3), C'(5, -1).

Worked Example: Q.6 — Point P(2, -9) rotated about the origin: find P' for 90 degrees clockwise, 180 degrees and 270 degrees clockwise.

Formula used: The three rotation rules.

Step 1: 90 degrees clockwise: (x, y) -> (y, -x): P' = (-9, -2).

Step 2: 180 degrees: (x, y) -> (-x, -y): P' = (-2, 9).

Step 3: 270 degrees clockwise: (x, y) -> (-y, x): P' = (9, 2).

Answer: P' = (-9, -2), (-2, 9) and (9, 2) respectively.

mcqs.q: Under a rotation of 90 degrees clockwise about the origin, P(5, 7) maps to:
mcqs.why: Rule for 90 degrees clockwise: (x, y) -> (y, -x). So (5, 7) -> (7, -5): swap the coordinates and change the sign of the new second coordinate.

mcqs.q: Under a rotation of 90 degrees clockwise about the origin, Q(-4, -7) maps to:
Under a rotation of 180 degrees about the origin, A(-1, 2) maps to:
mcqs.why: Rule for 180 degrees: (x, y) -> (-x, -y). So (-1, 2) -> (1, -2): both coordinates change sign, whichever direction (clockwise or anticlockwise) is used.

mcqs.q: Under a rotation of 270 degrees clockwise about the origin, P(2, -9) maps to:
mcqs.why: Rule for 270 degrees clockwise: (x, y) -> (-y, x). So (2, -9) -> (-(-9), 2) = (9, 2). (270 degrees clockwise is the same turn as 90 degrees anticlockwise.)

mcqs.q: Triangle A(-2, 1), B(3, 2), C(1, 5) rotated 90 degrees clockwise about the origin has image vertices:
Under a rotation of 90 degrees clockwise about the origin, R(-7, 5) maps to:
Under a rotation of 180 degrees about the origin, P(-5, -3) maps to:
The square (1, 1), (4, 1), (4, 4), (1, 4) rotated 90 degrees clockwise about the origin lands in which quadrant?
mcqs.why: Images under (x, y) -> (y, -x) are (1, -1), (1, -4), (4, -4), (4, -1): x positive, y negative — Quadrant IV.

mcqs.q: To FIND the centre of rotation from an object and its image, you draw:
options: The angle bisectors of the triangle
The perpendicular bisectors of the segments joining each vertex to its image — they meet at the centre
mcqs.why: The centre of rotation is equidistant from each point and its image, so it lies on the perpendicular bisector of every joining segment AA', BB', CC'. All these bisectors meet at the centre of rotation.

mcqs.q: Under a rotation of 90 degrees clockwise about the origin, S(2, -5) maps to:
mcqs.why: Rule for 90 degrees clockwise: (x, y) -> (y, -x). Swap the coordinates of (2, -5) and change the sign of the new second coordinate: (2, -5) -> (-5, -2).

lessons.title: Exercise: Enlargement (p.170-172)
lessons.notes_html:
An enlargement changes a figure's size by a scale factor from a fixed centre of enlargement: every image point lies on the ray from the centre through the object point, at (scale factor) times the distance. About a general centre, the rule is: image = centre + scale factor x (vertex - centre). About the origin this simplifies to multiplying both coordinates by the scale factor: (x, y) -> (kx, ky). To find the centre from a figure and its image, join corresponding vertices and extend — the lines meet at the centre; the scale factor is (image length)/(object length), or the ratio of distances from the centre.

Formula: Image point = centre + k x (vertex - centre), where k is the scale factor. Worked example from the book: triangle A(2, 1), B(3, 1), C(2, 3) enlarged by scale factor 3 about (1, 0) gives A'(4, 3), B'(7, 3), C'(4, 9).

In this exercise: 1. Enlarge a figure by scale factor 3 about (0, 0).; 2. Enlarge a rectangle by scale factor 2 about (-1, -3).; 3. Enlarge a figure by scale factor 3 about (-1, -1).; 4. Find the scale factor and centre of enlargement of given shapes. (Questions 1-4 use figures printed on grids; the method and rules above are applied vertex by vertex.)

Worked Example: Book's example — Enlarge triangle A(2, 1), B(3, 1), C(2, 3) by scale factor 3 about the centre (1, 0).

Formula used: image = centre + 3 x (vertex - centre).

Step 1: A: (1 + 3(2 - 1), 0 + 3(1 - 0)) = (1 + 3, 3) = (4, 3).

Step 2: B: (1 + 3(3 - 1), 0 + 3(1 - 0)) = (1 + 6, 3) = (7, 3).

Step 3: C: (1 + 3(2 - 1), 0 + 3(3 - 0)) = (4, 9).

Answer: A'(4, 3), B'(7, 3), C'(4, 9).

Worked Example: Q.2 rule — Enlargement by scale factor 2 about the centre (-1, -3): where does a vertex (x, y) go?

Formula used: image = centre + 2 x (vertex - centre).

Step 1: x-coordinate: -1 + 2(x - (-1)) = -1 + 2(x + 1) = 2x + 1.

Step 2: y-coordinate: -3 + 2(y - (-3)) = -3 + 2(y + 3) = 2y + 3.

Answer: Every vertex (x, y) moves to (2x + 1, 2y + 3).

mcqs.q: Enlarging by scale factor 3 about the origin sends (x, y) to:
mcqs.why: About the origin, the centre is (0, 0), so image = 0 + 3 x ((x, y) - 0) = (3x, 3y): both coordinates are multiplied by the scale factor.

mcqs.q: Triangle A(2, 1), B(3, 1), C(2, 3) enlarged by scale factor 3 about (1, 0) gives A' at:
In the same enlargement (scale factor 3 about (1, 0)), C(2, 3) maps to:
mcqs.why: C' = (1 + 3(2 - 1), 0 + 3(3 - 0)) = (1 + 3, 9) = (4, 9). The distance from the centre is tripled in each direction.

mcqs.q: Enlargement by scale factor 2 about the centre (-1, -3) sends (x, y) to:
mcqs.why: image = centre + 2(vertex - centre): x: -1 + 2(x + 1) = 2x + 1; y: -3 + 2(y + 3) = 2y + 3. So (x, y) -> (2x + 1, 2y + 3).

mcqs.q: Enlargement by scale factor 3 about the centre (-1, -1) sends (x, y) to:
mcqs.why: image = centre + 3(vertex - centre): x: -1 + 3(x + 1) = 3x + 2; y: -1 + 3(y + 1) = 3y + 2. So (x, y) -> (3x + 2, 3y + 2).

mcqs.q: Review Q.14: enlargement by scale factor 3 about (1, 1) sends (x, y) to:
mcqs.why: image = (1 + 3(x - 1), 1 + 3(y - 1)) = (3x - 2, 3y - 2). Always work from the centre: subtract it, multiply by k, add it back.

mcqs.q: The scale factor of an enlargement is found by:
options: Image length divided by corresponding object length
Object length divided by image length
mcqs.why: Scale factor = (length of any side of the image) / (corresponding side of the object) — equivalently, distance from centre to image point divided by distance from centre to object point. Angles do not change under enlargement.

mcqs.q: To find the CENTRE of enlargement from a figure and its image, you:
options: Join corresponding vertices and extend the lines — they meet at the centre
Draw perpendicular bisectors of the sides
mcqs.why: Every image point lies on the ray from the centre through its object point, so the lines AA', BB', CC' all pass through the centre of enlargement; their meeting point is the centre. (Perpendicular bisectors are for finding a centre of ROTATION.)

mcqs.q: A scale factor between 0 and 1 (for example 1/2) produces an image that is:
mcqs.why: Distances from the centre are multiplied by the factor: k > 1 enlarges, k = 1 keeps the size, and 0 < k < 1 shrinks the figure — still called an enlargement with a fractional scale factor.

mcqs.q: Under any enlargement, the image is ______ the object.
mcqs.why: Enlargement keeps all angles equal and multiplies all lengths by one factor, so corresponding sides are proportional — the definition of similar figures. It is congruent only when the scale factor is 1.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 11 (p.174-177)
lessons.notes_html:
This review covers Unit 11: congruent figures (same shape and size; symbol = with ~ above) and similar figures (same shape, different size; symbol ~); constructions of squares, rhombuses, parallelograms, trapezia, kites, rectangles and triangles; centres of rotation; and enlargements.

Formula: A rhombus drawn from its diagonals: the diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so each side = sqrt((d1/2)^2 + (d2/2)^2) — for diagonals 8 cm and 6 cm, side = sqrt(16 + 9) = 5 cm. A square from its diagonal d has side d/sqrt(2) — for d = 8 cm, side = 5.66 cm.

In this exercise: 1. Tick the correct option (10 MCQs on congruent/similar).; 2-9. Constructions: square, square from diagonal, rhombus, rhombus from diagonals, parallelogram, trapezium, kite, rectangle.; 10-11. Triangle constructions (SAS, SSS).; 12-13. Centres of rotation.; 14-15. Enlargements.

Worked Example: Q.5 — Draw rhombus ABCD with diagonals AC = 8 cm and BD = 6 cm (described).

Step 1: Draw AC = 8 cm. (Key point: the book prints the second diagonal as 'CD = 6 cm' — a diagonal of rhombus ABCD must join opposite vertices, so it is read as BD = 6 cm.)

Step 2: Draw the perpendicular bisector of AC, meeting it at O.

Step 3: With O as centre, draw arcs of radius 3 cm (half of BD) on the bisector on both sides, giving B and D.

Step 4: Join A to B, B to C, C to D and D to A.

Answer: Rhombus ABCD is constructed; the diagonals bisect each other at right angles and each side is 5 cm.

Worked Example: Q.3 — Construct a square whose diagonal is 8 cm (described).

Step 1: Draw the diagonal PR = 8 cm and its perpendicular bisector, meeting at the midpoint O.

Step 2: With O as centre, draw arcs of radius 4 cm (half the diagonal) on the bisector on both sides, giving Q and S.

Step 3: Join P to Q, Q to R, R to S and S to P.

Answer: Square PQRS is constructed; each side is 8/sqrt(2) = 5.66 cm.

mcqs.q: When the shape AND size of two figures are exactly the same, the figures are called:
mcqs.why: Congruent figures are exactly the same in shape and size — one can be placed exactly on top of the other. Similar figures share only the shape.

mcqs.q: When two figures have the same shape but different sizes, they are called:
mcqs.why: Similar figures: corresponding angles equal, corresponding sides in the same ratio, but the sizes differ. The symbol between similar figures is ~.

mcqs.q: The symbol used between two similar figures is:
mcqs.why: Similarity is written with the single tilde ~. Congruence uses the combined symbol (= with ~ above), because congruent figures are both similar AND equal in size.

mcqs.q: In congruent figures, corresponding angles and sides are:
mcqs.why: Congruence means exact sameness: every corresponding angle is equal and every corresponding side is equal. Proportionality without equality is similarity.

mcqs.q: In similar figures, corresponding sides are:
mcqs.why: For similar figures the corresponding angles are equal and the lengths of corresponding sides are proportional — each is the other multiplied by the scale factor.

mcqs.q: A square is constructed from its diagonal of 8 cm. Each side of the square is:
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras, side^2 + side^2 = diagonal^2, so side = diagonal/sqrt(2) = 8/1.414 = 5.66 cm. The construction marks half-diagonals of 4 cm on the perpendicular bisector.

mcqs.q: A rhombus has diagonals 8 cm and 6 cm. Each side of the rhombus is:
mcqs.why: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, giving four right triangles with legs 4 cm and 3 cm. Side = sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(25) = 5 cm.

mcqs.q: In Review Q.5, the book prints the rhombus's second diagonal as 'CD = 6 cm'. It must be read as BD because:
options: C and D are adjacent vertices — a diagonal joins OPPOSITE vertices
CD is a side of length 8 cm
The first diagonal is always AC in every figure
mcqs.why: In rhombus ABCD the vertices go around in order, so C and D are adjacent — CD is a side, not a diagonal. The diagonals are AC and BD, so the 6 cm diagonal is BD.

mcqs.q: A triangle with sides 7 cm and 10 cm and the INCLUDED angle 45 degrees is constructed by:
mcqs.why: The 45-degree angle lies between the two given sides (it is the included angle), so the construction is SAS: draw one side, make 45 degrees at its end, cut the arm with the other side's length, and join.

mcqs.q: In Review Q.15 the enlargement has a NEGATIVE scale factor. This tells us:
options: The image lies on the opposite side of the centre and is inverted
The scale factor was measured wrongly
mcqs.why: A negative scale factor means each image point is on the opposite ray through the centre — the image is inverted (turned) relative to the object, as found from the printed figure where AA', BB', CC' meet at the centre with the image on the far side.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.1 (p.189-191) - Types of Data, Graphs, Range, Variance and Standard Deviation
lessons.notes_html:
Discrete data is counted in whole numbers (marks, wickets, family members, pages). Continuous data is measured and can take decimal values (heights, weights). Ungrouped data is raw, unarranged data; grouped data is arranged in class intervals with frequencies. Graph choice: a pie graph shows parts of a whole; a bar graph compares categories; a multiple bar graph compares two categories together (e.g. brands across years); a pictograph suits simple category counts.

Formula: Range = xmax - xmin. Variance S^2 = (sum of x^2)/n - ((sum of x)/n)^2. Standard deviation S = sqrt(variance). Pie-chart angle = (value / total) x 360 degrees.

In this exercise: 1. Discrete or continuous?; 2. Grouped or ungrouped?; 3. Choose the best graph and conclude (with pie-chart angles).; 4-6. Range, variance and standard deviation.

Worked Example: Q.4(i) — Find the range, variance and standard deviation of 10, 14, 16, 18, 20, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19 (plants planted).

Formula used: Range = xmax - xmin; S^2 = Sx^2/n - (Sx/n)^2; S = sqrt(S^2).

Step 1: Range = 20 - 10 = 10.

Step 2: Sum of values Sx = 153; sum of squares Sx^2 = 2441; n = 10.

Step 3: S^2 = 2441/10 - (153/10)^2 = 244.10 - 234.09 = 10.01.

Step 4: S = sqrt(10.01) = 3.16.

Answer: Range = 10, Variance = 10.01, Standard deviation = 3.16.

Worked Example: Q.3(iii) — Employees: Engineers 50, Supervisors 80, Technicians 100, Labour 500 (total 730). Find the pie-chart angles.

Formula used: Angle = (value / total) x 360 degrees. A pie graph fits because the data shows parts of a whole.

Step 1: Engineers: (50/730) x 360 = 24.66 degrees. Supervisors: (80/730) x 360 = 39.45 degrees.

Step 2: Technicians: (100/730) x 360 = 49.32 degrees. Labour: (500/730) x 360 = 246.58 degrees.

Step 3: Check: 24.66 + 39.45 + 49.32 + 246.58 = 360 degrees. Conclusion: Labour is by far the largest group.

Answer: Angles 24.66, 39.45, 49.32 and 246.58 degrees.

Key point: In Q.3(v) the book prints Honda's 2022 bike sales as 8000; read with the pattern of the table (1100/1000/800 for 2024/2023/2022) it is 800.

mcqs.q: The heights of 10 students (5.3, 6.4, 5.5, ... feet) are an example of:
mcqs.why: Height is MEASURED, not counted, and can take any decimal value (5.3, 5.55, ...). Measured data that can take decimal values is continuous data.

mcqs.q: The wickets taken by Shaheen in ten matches (4, 0, 1, 3, ...) are:
mcqs.why: Wickets are counted in whole numbers — you cannot take 2.5 wickets in this count. Countable whole-number data is discrete data.

mcqs.q: Thirty students' marks arranged in class intervals 1-10, 11-20, ..., 71-80 with frequencies are:
mcqs.why: Data arranged in class intervals with frequencies is grouped data. The same marks written as a raw list would be ungrouped.

mcqs.q: For parts of a whole (employees of a company, total given), the most appropriate graph is:
mcqs.why: A pie graph divides a circle into sectors proportional to each part of the whole: angle = (value/total) x 360 degrees. Bar graphs compare separate categories rather than shares of a total.

mcqs.q: In the employees pie chart (total 730), the angle for Labour (500) is:
mcqs.why: Angle = (500/730) x 360 = 180000/730 = 246.58 degrees. Labour is more than two-thirds of the whole, so its sector is more than 240 degrees. All four angles sum to 360 degrees.

mcqs.q: For comparing bike sales of 4 brands across 3 years together, the best graph is:
mcqs.why: Two categories (brand AND year) must be compared together, so a multiple bar graph — grouped bars for each brand, one bar per year — is most appropriate. Conclusion from it: Honda sold best every year.
Range = xmax - xmin = 20 - 10 = 10. (15.3 is the MEAN of the data, not the range.)

mcqs.q: For the same data (sum x = 153, sum x^2 = 2441, n = 10), the variance is:
mcqs.why: S^2 = Sx^2/n - (Sx/n)^2 = 2441/10 - (15.3)^2 = 244.10 - 234.09 = 10.01. (3.16 is the standard deviation, the square root of the variance.)

mcqs.q: The standard deviation is:
options: The square root of the variance
mcqs.why: S = sqrt(S^2). For variance 10.01, S = sqrt(10.01) = 3.16. Standard deviation is in the same units as the data; variance is in squared units.

mcqs.q: Marks of ten students: 60, 88, 95, 90, 80, 85, 80, 70, 75, 65. The range, variance and standard deviation are:

lessons.title: Exercise 12.2 (p.199-200) - Frequency Tables, Histograms and Frequency Polygons
lessons.notes_html:
A frequency distribution table counts how often each value (or class) occurs; the frequencies must add up to the total number of values. A histogram shows grouped data with rectangles on the class boundaries (e.g. classes 20-29, 30-39 are drawn on boundaries 19.5-29.5, 29.5-39.5) with no gaps between bars and heights equal to the frequencies. A frequency polygon plots (class midpoint, frequency) points joined by straight segments, closed at the axis with extra midpoints of frequency 0.

Formula: Class midpoint = (lower limit + upper limit) / 2. Class boundary = limit -/+ 0.5 when classes have a gap of 1.

In this exercise: 1. Frequency table of weights.; 2. Grouped table for class-test marks.; 3. Tables with class sizes 100 and 5.; 4. Histogram of park visitors.; 5. Frequency polygon for the Cost of Living Index.; 6. Reading a printed histogram (method given — the bar heights appear only in the picture).; 7. Histogram of teachers' salaries.

Worked Example: Q.2 — Marks of 25 students out of 30 (values from 15 to 29). Make a grouped table with classes of width 5.

Formula used: Count the values falling in each class; check the total.

Step 1: Classes: 15-19, 20-24, 25-29.

Step 2: 15-19 has 9 students (15, 15, 16 and six 19s); 20-24 has 2 students (20, 21); 25-29 has 14 students.

Step 3: Check: 9 + 2 + 14 = 25. Correct.

Answer: 15-19: 9, 20-24: 2, 25-29: 14. The highest-marks group (25-29) has 14 students; the single highest mark, 29, was obtained by 1 student.

Worked Example: Q.5 — Draw a frequency polygon for the Cost of Living Index: 120-125: 2, 125-130: 8, 130-135: 14, 135-140: 20, 140-145: 10, 145-150: 6 (described).

Formula used: Midpoint = (lower + upper)/2.

Step 1: Midpoints: 122.5, 127.5, 132.5, 137.5, 142.5, 147.5.

Step 2: Plot the points (122.5, 2), (127.5, 8), (132.5, 14), (137.5, 20), (142.5, 10), (147.5, 6).

Step 3: Join with straight segments and close the polygon at the axis using the midpoints 117.5 and 152.5 at frequency 0.

Answer: The polygon passes through those six points, peaking at (137.5, 20).

mcqs.q: In the weights table of 20 students (30, 39, 36, 42, ...), the weight 38 kg has frequency:
mcqs.why: Counting the list: 38 appears in positions 5, 9 and 14 — 3 times. The full table (30:1, 34:1, 35:1, 36:2, 38:3, 39:3, 41:3, 42:3, 44:2, 45:1) sums to 20, as it must.

mcqs.q: For the class-test marks (25 students), the grouped table with classes 15-19, 20-24, 25-29 is:
mcqs.why: 15-19: the two 15s, one 16 and six 19s = 9. 20-24: only 20 and 21 = 2. 25-29: the remaining 14. Check: 9 + 2 + 14 = 25 students.

mcqs.q: How many students are in the highest-marks group (25-29), and how many scored the single highest mark 29?
options: 14 students in the group; 1 student scored 29
mcqs.why: The class 25-29 collects all marks from 25 to 29: 14 students. Within it, the mark 29 itself occurs only once in the list.

mcqs.q: With class size 100 for the 30 values in Q.3(a), the class 500-599 has frequency:
In a histogram, the bars are drawn:
options: With gaps between them, like a bar graph
On the class boundaries with NO gaps between bars
mcqs.why: A histogram represents continuous grouped data: rectangles stand on the class boundaries (e.g. 19.5-29.5) side by side with no gaps, and each bar's height equals its class frequency.

mcqs.q: Classes 20-29, 30-39 in a histogram are drawn on the boundaries:
mcqs.why: The classes have a gap of 1 (29 to 30), so each boundary is adjusted by half the gap, 0.5: 20 - 0.5 = 19.5 and 29 + 0.5 = 29.5, making the classes continuous so the bars touch.

mcqs.q: The midpoint of the class 135-140 is:
mcqs.why: Midpoint = (lower limit + upper limit)/2 = (135 + 140)/2 = 275/2 = 137.5. Frequency polygons are plotted at midpoints — here the point is (137.5, 20).

mcqs.q: A frequency polygon is closed at the axis by:
options: Joining the first and last points directly
Adding the midpoints of the classes before the first and after the last, at frequency 0
mcqs.why: For the Cost of Living data the polygon is closed with the extra midpoints 117.5 and 152.5 at frequency 0, so the polygon meets the axis one class-width beyond each end.

mcqs.q: For the teachers' salaries histogram (50000-55000: 8, ..., 65000-70000: 10, ...), the tallest bar is for:
mcqs.why: The frequencies are 8, 6, 9, 10, 6, 5. The largest frequency, 10, belongs to the class Rs 65000-70000, so its bar is the tallest.

mcqs.q: The first check on any frequency table is:
options: The frequencies must add up to the total number of values
The classes must be of width 10
The largest frequency must be in the middle
mcqs.why: Frequencies count every value exactly once, so their sum must equal n, the number of data values (20, 25, 30 in this exercise's tables). A different sum means a counting error.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 12 (p.201-202)
lessons.notes_html:
This review covers Unit 12: data types, frequency tables, histograms, frequency polygons, range, variance and standard deviation.

Formula: Variance S^2 = Sx^2/n - (Sx/n)^2; Standard deviation = sqrt(variance); Range = xmax - xmin; Frequency = number of occurrences of a value.

In this exercise: 1. Tick the correct option (10 MCQs).; 2-3. Frequency tables.; 4. Histograms.; 5-6. Frequency polygons.

Worked Example: Q.5 — Frequency polygon for the pages of 30 library books, grouped in classes of width 30 (described).

Formula used: Count each class, then plot (midpoint, frequency).

Step 1: Classes and frequencies: 90-119: 11, 120-149: 2, 150-179: 4, 180-209: 10, 210-239: 3. Check: 11 + 2 + 4 + 10 + 3 = 30.

Step 2: Midpoints: 104.5, 134.5, 164.5, 194.5, 224.5.

Step 3: Plot (104.5, 11), (134.5, 2), (164.5, 4), (194.5, 10), (224.5, 3) and join with straight segments.

Answer: The polygon passes through those five points.

Worked Example: Q.2 — Frequency table for the weights of 25 students in classes of width 10.

Formula used: Count the values in each class 30-39, 40-49, 50-59, 60-69, 70-79.

Step 1: 30-39: 5; 40-49: 4; 50-59: 4.

Step 2: 60-69: 6; 70-79: 6. Check: 5 + 4 + 4 + 6 + 6 = 25.

Answer: 30-39: 5 ; 40-49: 4 ; 50-59: 4 ; 60-69: 6 ; 70-79: 6.

mcqs.q: Data which is quantitative and countable is called:
mcqs.why: Countable data in whole numbers (pages of a book, students, goals) is discrete data. Measurable data that can take any value in a range is continuous.

mcqs.q: The weights of students (in kg) are:
mcqs.why: Weight is measured on a scale and can be 42.5 kg, 42.55 kg, ... — it can take decimal values, so it is continuous data. (Whether it is grouped depends on how it is arranged, not on the quantity.)

mcqs.q: Data collected directly and not arranged is called:
mcqs.why: Raw data in its original, unarranged form is ungrouped data. Arranging it into classes with frequencies produces grouped data (a frequency distribution).

mcqs.q: The variance formula is:
mcqs.why: Variance S^2 = (sum of squares)/n MINUS (mean)^2 = Sx^2/n - (Sx/n)^2. The standard deviation is the square root of this quantity.

mcqs.q: Range is:
mcqs.why: Range = largest value - smallest value = xmax - xmin. It measures the spread of the data and is never negative.

mcqs.q: The number of occurrences of a value is called its:
mcqs.why: Frequency = how many times a value (or class) occurs in the data. The frequencies of all values add up to the total number of observations.

mcqs.q: In Q.2's table (weights of 25 students), the classes 60-69 and 70-79 each have frequency:
mcqs.why: Counting the list: 60-69 contains 60, 61, 65, 64, 67, 66 = 6 students; 70-79 contains 70, 71, 72, 73, 74, 75 = 6 students. The whole table 5 + 4 + 4 + 6 + 6 = 25.

mcqs.q: In Q.3's frequency table (marks of 30 students), the marks 15 and 16 each have frequency:
mcqs.why: Mark 15 occurs 3 times and mark 16 occurs 3 times in the list. (The full table sums to 30; the most frequent marks are 15 and 16.)

mcqs.q: For the histogram data of Q.4(i) grouped in classes of width 10, the class 40-49 has frequency:
mcqs.why: Values in 40-49: 43, 42, 40, 44, 46, 48, 49 = 7 values — the tallest bar of that histogram. The full table is 1, 5, 7, 3, 4, 4, 3, 3 = 30 values.

mcqs.q: For Q.6's frequency polygon (classes 91-100 up to 131-140), the points are plotted at midpoints:

lessons.title: Exercise 13.1 (p.210-211) - Probability Basics
lessons.notes_html:
The probability of an event measures how likely it is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). For equally likely outcomes, P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes. Experimental probability uses actual trial results: P = (number of times the event occurred) / (total trials). Events with the same probability are equally likely.

Formula: P = n(E) / n(S), where n(E) is the number of favourable outcomes and n(S) the total number of outcomes in the sample space.

In this exercise: 1. Socks picked without looking.; 2. Two dice — getting 3 and 4.; 3. Combinations of two vegetables.; 4. Left-handed students.; 5. A stone green or purple.; 6-7. Goal probabilities and equally likely events.; 8. Fruit on a plate.; 9. Experimental probability from 50 coin tosses.; 10. A 6-sector spinner.

Worked Example: Q.5 — A box contains 20 red, 25 green and 30 purple stones. Find the probability that a stone drawn at random is green or purple.

Formula used: P = favourable outcomes / total outcomes.

Step 1: Total stones = 20 + 25 + 30 = 75.

Step 2: Favourable (green or purple) = 25 + 30 = 55.

Step 3: P = 55/75 = 11/15 (dividing by 5).

Answer: Probability = 11/15.

Worked Example: Q.2 — Two dice are rolled. Find the probability of getting 3 and 4 (in any order).

Formula used: P = favourable / total, with total = 6 x 6 = 36.

Step 1: Total outcomes for two dice = 36.

Step 2: Favourable outcomes: (3, 4) and (4, 3) — 2 outcomes, because the dice can show 3-then-4 or 4-then-3.

Step 3: P = 2/36 = 1/18.

Answer: Probability = 1/18.

mcqs.q: You have 6 pairs of white socks and 3 pairs of black socks. The probability of picking a white pair without looking is:
mcqs.why: Total pairs = 6 + 3 = 9. P(white) = 6/9 = 2/3. (P(black) = 3/9 = 1/3, and 2/3 + 1/3 = 1 as it must.)

mcqs.q: Two dice are rolled. The probability of getting 3 and 4 (in any order) is:
mcqs.why: Total outcomes = 6 x 6 = 36. Favourable: (3, 4) and (4, 3) = 2 outcomes. P = 2/36 = 1/18.

mcqs.q: Aimen chooses two vegetables from Peas, Carrots and Potato. The number of possible combinations is:
mcqs.why: The combinations are {Peas, Carrots}, {Peas, Potato} and {Carrots, Potato} — 3 combinations. Order does not matter when choosing a pair.

mcqs.q: In Grade-VIII, 10 out of 60 students are left-handed. The probability that a student is left-handed is:
mcqs.why: P = favourable / total = 10/60 = 1/6 (dividing numerator and denominator by 10).

mcqs.q: A box has 20 red, 25 green and 30 purple stones. P(green or purple) is:
mcqs.why: Total = 75 stones. Green or purple = 25 + 30 = 55 favourable stones. P = 55/75 = 11/15 after dividing by 5.

mcqs.q: In a match of 6 goals, team A scored 2 and team B scored 4. P(a goal was team A's) and P(team B's) are:
mcqs.why: P(A) = 2/6 = 1/3 and P(B) = 4/6 = 2/3. The two probabilities sum to 1 because every goal belongs to one of the two teams.

mcqs.q: Ahmed and Waqas scored one goal each; Sajid scored 2; total goals 8. Which events are equally likely?
mcqs.why: P(Ahmed) = 1/8 and P(Waqas) = 1/8 — equal, so their events are equally likely. Sajid's probability is 2/8 = 1/4, which is different.

mcqs.q: A plate has one apple, one orange and 2 mangoes. P(picking a mango) is:
mcqs.why: Total fruits = 1 + 1 + 2 = 4. Mangoes = 2. P = 2/4 = 1/2.

mcqs.q: A coin was tossed 50 times: Head came 38 times, Tail 12 times. The experimental probabilities are:
mcqs.why: Experimental P = occurrences / trials: Head = 38/50 = 0.76 (76%), Tail = 12/50 = 0.24 (24%). Experimental probability comes from observed results, not from the theoretical 1/2.

mcqs.q: A spinner has 6 equal sectors labelled a, b, b, c, a, d. P(a), P(b) and P(c) are:
mcqs.why: Out of 6 sectors: a appears twice (2/6 = 1/3), b appears twice (2/6 = 1/3), c appears once (1/6), and d appears once (1/6). Total: 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 1.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 13 (p.212-213)
lessons.notes_html:
This review covers Unit 13: equally likely events (same probability), mutually exclusive events (cannot happen together), independent events (one does not affect the other), dependent events (one affects the other), simple combined events, sample spaces, and theoretical and experimental probability.

Formula: Theoretical probability P = n(E) / n(S). Sample space of two coins: {HH, HT, TH, TT}; of one die: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.

In this exercise: 1. Tick the correct option (10 MCQs).; 2-3. Sample spaces of two coins and a die.; 4. Exactly two heads in three coin flips.; 5. Selecting a girl.; 6. A ball red or green.; 7. Multiples of 3 and 4 from 1 to 20.; 8. Equally likely or not?; 9. Experimental probabilities from 18 die rolls.; 10. Dependent events in a football match.

Worked Example: Q.4 — What is the probability of getting exactly two heads when flipping three coins?

Formula used: P = favourable / total.

Step 1: Sample space has 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT.

Step 2: Exactly two heads: HHT, HTH, THH — 3 outcomes.

Step 3: P = 3/8.

Answer: Probability = 3/8.

Worked Example: Q.9 — Ahmed rolled a die 18 times; the outcomes 1-6 had frequencies 4, 3, 1, 2, 4, 4. Find the experimental P(2), P(4) and P(6).

Formula used: Experimental P = frequency / total trials (18).

Step 1: P(2) = 3/18 = 1/6. P(4) = 2/18 = 1/9.

Step 2: P(6) = 4/18 = 2/9.

Step 3: Outcomes 1, 5 and 6 each occurred 4 times, so in this experiment they are equally likely; any two different numbers on a single roll are mutually exclusive (they cannot occur together).

Answer: P(2) = 1/6, P(4) = 1/9, P(6) = 2/9.

Key points: In Review MCQ (ii), A = {H} and B = {T} are also equally likely, but the property the book tests is that they cannot occur together — mutually exclusive. In MCQ (iv), A = {2, 4, 6} and B = {1, 2, 3} both have probability 1/2, so by the book's example they are equally likely (they are NOT mutually exclusive — both contain 2). In Q.10, goals from one fixed total of 12 are dependent events: the more one player scores, the fewer remain for the others.

mcqs.q: If S = {H, T}, A = {H} and B = {T}, the events A and B are (as the book tests here):
options: Mutually exclusive — they cannot occur together
mcqs.why: A single toss cannot be both Head and Tail, so A and B cannot occur at the same time: mutually exclusive events. (They happen to be equally likely too, but mutual exclusivity is the property tested.)

mcqs.q: If S = {1,...,6}, A = {2, 4, 6} and B = {1, 2, 3}, the events A and B are called (by the book's example):
mcqs.why: P(A) = 3/6 = 1/2 and P(B) = 3/6 = 1/2 — equal probabilities, so the events are equally likely. They are not mutually exclusive because the outcome 2 belongs to both.

mcqs.q: If the occurrence of one event does NOT affect the other, the events are called:
mcqs.why: Independent events: one happening does not change the probability of the other (for example, two separate coin tosses). If one event DOES affect the other, they are dependent.

mcqs.q: Ahmed rolls a fair die. The probability of getting 6 is:
mcqs.why: A fair die has 6 equally likely outcomes {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} and only one of them is 6: P = n(E)/n(S) = 1/6.

mcqs.q: The formula of theoretical probability is:
mcqs.why: P(E) = (number of favourable outcomes) / (total number of outcomes) = n(E)/n(S). It always lies between 0 and 1.

mcqs.q: The probability of getting exactly two heads when flipping three coins is:
mcqs.why: The sample space has 8 outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT. Exactly two heads occurs in HHT, HTH, THH — 3 outcomes. P = 3/8.

mcqs.q: A class has 10 boys and 15 girls. The probability of selecting a girl is:
mcqs.why: Total students = 10 + 15 = 25. P(girl) = 15/25 = 3/5 after dividing by 5.

mcqs.q: A bag contains 3 red, 4 green and 5 blue balls. P(red or green) is:
mcqs.why: Total balls = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12. Red or green = 3 + 4 = 7 balls. P = 7/12.

mcqs.q: A number is chosen at random from {1, 2, ..., 20}. P(multiple of 3) and P(multiple of 4) are:
mcqs.why: Multiples of 3 up to 20: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 — 6 numbers, P = 6/20 = 3/10. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 — 5 numbers, P = 5/20 = 1/4.

mcqs.q: In Q.10's match (12 goals total; Iqbal 2, Hussain 2, Waseem 3), the players' scoring events are dependent because:
options: The goals share one fixed total — the more one player scores, the fewer remain for the others
Each player scored the same number
mcqs.why: All goals come out of the same fixed total of 12, so one player's scoring affects what is left for the others — the events are dependent. (Iqbal's and Hussain's events are equally likely, each 2/12 = 1/6, but no pair here is independent.)
